title: Green’s theorem
objectives: Turn a line integral around a closed curve into a double integral with Green’s theorem.

screens.title: Round a square
screens.prose: The rotation field $(-y, x)$ again, round the unit square $[0, 1] \times [0, 1]$, counterclockwise. Work out the work on each side, as in lesson 3.
screens.question: Fill in each side's work and the total.

hints.text: On the bottom $y = 0$, so $\mathbf F = (0, t)$, at right angles to $(1, 0)$.
On the right $\mathbf F = (-t, 1)$ and $\mathbf r' = (0, 1)$: integrand 1.
On the top $\mathbf F = (-1, 1 - t)$ and $\mathbf r' = (-1, 0)$: integrand 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Dot $\mathbf F$ with each side's direction.

byKey.sign: On the top the motion is $(-1, 0)$ and $\mathbf F = (-1, 1 - t)$: the dot product is $+1$.

explain.text: The right and top sides each give 1, the others 0. The total 2 equals the curl 2 times the area 1.

screens.title: Round a circle
screens.prose: Round the unit circle the same field gave $2\pi$ in lesson 3. Its curl is $Q_x - P_y = 2$ everywhere, and the disc's area is $\pi$. The square gave 2, with curl 2 and area 1.
screens.question: What does the circulation equal in both cases?

options.text: The curl times the area enclosed
The curl times the length of the boundary
options.why: The circle's length is $2\pi$, and $2 \times 2\pi = 4\pi$, not $2\pi$.
The square has area 1 but circulation 2.
The square's boundary is 4 long, but its circulation is 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each option on both shapes.

explain.text: Both loops give curl times area. With a constant curl that product is the double integral of the curl. Green's theorem says this holds for any curl.

screens.title: Green's theorem for a rectangle
screens.prose: **Green's theorem.** Let $C$ be a piecewise smooth simple closed curve bounding $D$, traversed counterclockwise with $D$ on the left. Let $P$, $Q$ have continuous partials on an open set containing $D$. Then $$\oint_C P\,dx + Q\,dy = \iint_D (Q_x - P_y)\,dA.$$ Prove the $P$ part for $D = [a, b] \times [c, d]$.
screens.question: Arrange the proof that $\oint_C P\,dx = \iint_D -P_y\,dA$.

lines.text: $\iint_D -P_y\,dA = \int_a^b \left[-P(x, d) + P(x, c)\right]dx$. (Integrate in $y$ first; fundamental theorem.)
The bottom side gives $\int_a^b P(x, c)\,dx$ to $\oint P\,dx$. (Traversed left to right.)
The top side gives $-\int_a^b P(x, d)\,dx$. (Traversed right to left.)
The vertical sides give 0 to $\oint P\,dx$. ($dx = 0$ there.)
So $\oint_C P\,dx = \iint_D -P_y\,dA$; the $Q$ part is the same with $x$ and $y$ swapped. (Compare lines 1 to 4.)
The top side gives $+\int_a^b P(x, d)\,dx$. (Along the top.)
lines.why: Counterclockwise, the top runs from $x = b$ back to $x = a$, so its integral has a minus sign.

hints.text: Then add the four sides' contributions to $\oint P\,dx$.
The top runs right to left, so it carries a minus sign.

feedback.correct: Both sides equal $\int_a^b \left[P(x, c) - P(x, d)\right]dx$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line needs the reason beside it.

byKey.d1: You traversed the top left to right. Counterclockwise, it runs right to left.
byKey.left-out: All five true lines are needed.

explain.text: Integrating $-P_y$ in $y$ leaves $P$ on the bottom minus $P$ on the top. The boundary gives exactly those two terms, with the vertical sides adding 0. Swapping roles proves the $Q$ part.

screens.title: Use the curl
screens.prose: Take $\oint_C (x^2 - y)\,dx + (x + y^2)\,dy$ round the circle of radius 2, counterclockwise. A direct route needs four integrals; Green needs one.
screens.question: What is the circulation?

hints.text: The curl is 2 and the disc's area is $4\pi$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the curl, then multiply by the area.

byKey.unit: $2\pi$ uses the unit disc. This disc has radius 2 and area $4\pi$.
byKey.one: You took the curl as 1. $Q_x - P_y = 1 - (-1) = 2$.

explain.text: $Q_x - P_y = 1 + 1 = 2$, constant. So the circulation is $2 \times 4\pi = 8\pi \approx 25.13$, with no line integral done. Here area and length are both $4\pi$; only the area rule works at other radii.

screens.title: A half disc
screens.prose: Take $\oint_C y^2\,dx + 3xy\,dy$ round the upper half of the unit disc, counterclockwise. Its curl is $Q_x - P_y = 3y - 2y = y$. Use polar coordinates, $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$.
screens.question: What is $\oint_C y^2\,dx + 3xy\,dy$, to 3 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate $y = r\sin\theta$ with $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$.

byKey.no-r: You used $dA = dr\,d\theta$: $\int_0^1 r\,dr \times 2 = 1$. The polar area element is $r\,dr\,d\theta$.

explain.text: $\iint_D y\,dA = \tfrac13 \times 2 = \tfrac23$. The next screen checks it by the direct route.

screens.title: Check it directly
screens.prose: The boundary is the arc $(\cos t, \sin t)$, $0 \le t \le \pi$, then the diameter from $(-1, 0)$ to $(1, 0)$. On the arc the integrand is $-\sin^3 t + 3\cos^2 t\sin t$.
screens.question: Fill in each piece, to 3 decimal places.

hints.text: On the diameter $y = 0$ and $dy = 0$, so it gives 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the arc's two terms separately.

byKey.cube: You kept only $-\int \sin^3 t\,dt = -\tfrac43$. Add $\int 3\cos^2 t\sin t\,dt = 2$.

explain.text: The arc gives $-\tfrac43 + 2 = \tfrac23$ and the diameter 0, so the direct total is $\tfrac23$. Two routes, one answer.

screens.title: When there is no direct route
screens.prose: Take $\oint_C (e^{x^2} - y)\,dx + (x + \sin y^2)\,dy$ round the unit circle, counterclockwise. Neither $e^{x^2}$ nor $\sin y^2$ has an elementary antiderivative.
screens.question: What is the circulation?

hints.text: The curl is 2 and the area is $\pi$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The hard parts drop out of the curl.

byKey.zero: The $e^{x^2}$ and $\sin y^2$ parts contribute 0, but $-y$ and $x$ do not.

explain.text: $e^{x^2}$ depends on $x$ alone, so its $y$-derivative is 0; likewise $\sin y^2$. The curl is 2, so the circulation is $2\pi$.

screens.title: An open path
screens.prose: Green needs a closed curve. We want the rotation field's work along the upper unit semicircle from $(1, 0)$ to $(-1, 0)$. Close it with the diameter.
screens.question: What is the work along the semicircle, to 3 decimal places?

hints.text: Round the closed half disc, Green gives $2 \times \tfrac{\pi}{2}$.

feedback.correct: $\pi \approx 3.142$; directly, the integrand is 1 for $0 \le t \le \pi$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the diameter's work from the closed loop's.

byKey.full: $2\pi$ is the whole circle. The half disc has area $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$.
byKey.half: $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ is the area. Multiply by the curl 2.

explain.text: Green gives $2 \times \tfrac{\pi}{2} = \pi$ round the half disc. The diameter adds 0, so the semicircle carries all of $\pi$.

screens.title: Which formula
screens.prose: Back to $\oint_C y^2\,dx + 3xy\,dy$ round the upper half disc, counterclockwise. Four versions of Green's integrand are on offer.
screens.question: Which integrand gives the circulation?

options.why: You subtracted the wrong way round. That sign belongs to the clockwise loop.
You differentiated each entry by its own letter. Green crosses them: $Q$ by $x$, $P$ by $y$.
You added the partials. Green subtracts $P_y$.

feedback.correct: $Q_x - P_y = y$ and $\iint_D y\,dA = \tfrac23$, matching the direct route.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which version gave the direct route's $\tfrac23$?

byKey.rev: You swapped the subtraction. $P_y - Q_x$ gives the clockwise answer, $-\tfrac23$.
byKey.div: You used $Q_y - P_x$. Green's integrand is $Q_x - P_y$.

explain.text: Only $Q_x - P_y$ with a counterclockwise boundary matches the direct $\tfrac23$. Clockwise traversal or a swapped subtraction gives $-\tfrac23$.

screens.title: A region with a hole
screens.prose: An annulus has two boundary circles: the outer one counterclockwise, the inner one clockwise. The region stays on the left. The vortex of lesson 4 has curl 0 off the origin.
screens.question: What is the vortex's circulation round the circle of radius $\tfrac12$, counterclockwise?

options.text: $2\pi$, the same as round the circle of radius 2

options.why: The circle surrounds the hole, where Green does not apply to the whole disc.
Green on the annulus forces outer minus inner to be 0, so they are equal.

options.text: $-2\pi$, because the inner circle is clockwise
options.why: Clockwise is how the annulus uses it. Counterclockwise, it gives $+2\pi$.

hints.text: Apply Green to the annulus between radius $\tfrac12$ and 2.
The curl is 0 there, so outer counterclockwise plus inner clockwise is 0.
So the two counterclockwise circulations are equal.

feedback.correct: $2\pi$: every circle round the origin gives the same circulation.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use Green on the ring between the two circles.

explain.text: On the annulus Green gives outer minus inner $= \iint 0\,dA = 0$. So any counterclockwise simple loop round the origin gives $2\pi$, by the same step with a small circle. This is why lesson 4's test failed: the hole carries it.

screens.title: Both sides numerically
screens.prose: Write `circulation`, the line side of Green, with `quad`, and `curl_integral_polar`, the area side over a polar sector, with `dblquad`. The tests check this lesson's circle, half disc and vortex.
screens.question: Complete both functions.

widget.starter:
import math
from scipy.integrate import quad, dblquad


def circulation(P, Q, x, y, dx, dy, a, b):
    """Integral of P x'(t) + Q y'(t) for a <= t <= b.

    P, Q take (x, y); x, y, dx, dy take t.
    """
    pass


def curl_integral_polar(curl, r_max, theta0, theta1):
    """Integral of curl(x, y) over the polar region
    0 <= r <= r_max, theta0 <= theta <= theta1.

    dblquad(func, a, b, gfun, hfun) integrates func(inner, outer):
    the INNER variable comes first. Remember dA = r dr dtheta.
    """

examples.call: circulation(lambda x, y: x*x - y, lambda x, y: x + y*y, lambda t: 2*math.cos(t), lambda t: 2*math.sin(t), lambda t: -2*math.sin(t), lambda t: 2*math.cos(t), 0, 2*math.pi)

circulation(lambda x, y: y*y, lambda x, y: 3*x*y, lambda t: math.cos(t), lambda t: math.sin(t), lambda t: -math.sin(t), lambda t: math.cos(t), 0, math.pi)

circulation(lambda x, y: -y/(x*x + y*y), lambda x, y: x/(x*x + y*y), lambda t: 0.5*math.cos(t), lambda t: 0.5*math.sin(t), lambda t: -0.5*math.sin(t), lambda t: 0.5*math.cos(t), 0, 2*math.pi)

In `dblquad`, write `f(r, theta)` with `r` first, since `r` is the inner variable.
Multiply the curl by `r` for the area element.

feedback.correct: Both sides agree on every test, and the vortex gives $2\pi$ at both radii.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-4: Test 4 is the area side for the unit disc. Check the factor `r` and that `r` is the first argument of your inner function.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 integrates $y$ over the half disc; it should give $\tfrac23$.

screens.title: A round trip in prices
screens.prose: Lesson 3's rule holds $\mathbf h = (0, S_1 - 100)$. Prices go round a loop. Stock 1 rises from £100 to £110, then stock 2 from £100 to £105. Then each falls back to £100.
screens.question: Fill in each leg's P&L and the total.

hints.text: On leg 2 the rule holds 10 shares; on leg 4 it holds 0.

feedback.correct: £50, though prices end where they started. Green: curl 1 times area $10 \times 5$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the shares of stock 2 held on each of its legs.

byKey.no-hold: On leg 2, $S_1 = 110$, so the rule holds 10 shares of stock 2.
byKey.held: On leg 4, $S_1 = 100$, so the rule holds 0 shares: no loss.

explain.text: The loop earns £50. The holdings' curl is $Q_x - P_y = 1$ and the loop encloses $10 \times 5 = 50$ square pounds, counterclockwise. A gradient holding would have curl 0 and earn nothing round a loop.

ideas: Let $C$ be a piecewise smooth simple closed curve round $D$, counterclockwise. If $P$, $Q$ are continuously differentiable on an open set containing $D$, then $\oint_C P\,dx + Q\,dy = \iint_D (Q_x - P_y)\,dA$.
Use it when the curl is simpler than the boundary; close an open path and subtract the added piece.
A region with a hole has two boundary pieces, the inner one clockwise; the vortex's $2\pi$ lives in its hole.

formula.note: C counterclockwise, region on the left.

quiz.prose: A region is cut into rectangles, and Green's theorem holds on each one.
quiz.question: Why does it then hold on the whole region?

options.text: Each inner edge is traversed once each way, so those parts cancel
Areas add, so the boundaries add too
options.why: Boundaries do not simply add: the inner edges would be counted. They cancel because their directions are opposite.

options.text: The curl is the same in every rectangle
options.why: The curl may vary; the argument works for any curl.

options.text: The rectangles are small enough to ignore their edges
options.why: Size does not matter here: the inner edges cancel exactly.

feedback.correct: Inner edges cancel, leaving only the outer boundary.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow an edge shared by two rectangles.

explain.text: Adding the rectangles' double integrals gives the whole double integral. Each shared edge is crossed once in each direction, so its line integrals cancel, leaving the outer boundary.

quiz.prose: Round the price loop, $\mathbf h = (0, S_1 - 100)$ earned £50 with prices back where they started.
quiz.question: Why does the loop earn £50?

options.text: The holdings have curl 1, and the loop encloses area 50

options.why: They end exactly where they started.
A gradient's loop total is 0. This field has curl 1.
Costs would reduce it; they do not create it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply Green's theorem to the holdings field.

explain.text: By Green, the loop's P&L is $\iint (Q_x - P_y)\,dA = 1 \times 50 = 50$. Holdings that are a gradient would earn 0 round every loop.
